# Hard-to-vary report: the Time Traveller's argument for time travel

## 1. The question, frozen

The opening centers the excerpt on one claim, made by the Time Traveller and pressed by his listeners: **time travel should be possible, because time is a fourth dimension of the same kind as the three of space.** That is an *argument*, not a diagnosis or a design. Range: I test the reasoning in Chapter I through the model demonstration in Chapter II, where it is first offered in earnest. I do not test whether Wells wrote a good story, or whether the later journey "worked" as fiction — different questions, noted at the end but not tested here.

## 2. The explanation in parts

- **P1 — Duration-as-dimension.** An "instantaneous" cube cannot really exist, so any real body has Length, Breadth, Thickness *and* Duration.
- **P2 — Only-perception-differs.** Time and space differ only because our consciousness moves along the time-axis, one way, at a fixed rate; nothing else marks time out.
- **P3 — Gravity analogy.** We move freely in two spatial directions, and even the third (up/down) once technology (the balloon) got round the obstacle (gravitation); so our fixed "drift" through time might likewise be got round by a machine.
- **P4 — Supporting instances.** (a) A vivid memory is a momentary backward "jump" of the mind. (b) A barometer chart shows a line "along the Time-Dimension," proof that "time is only a kind of Space."
- **P5 — The demonstration.** The model vanishes when the lever is pressed, offered as "experimental verification."
- **P6 — The threshold patch.** When Filby's and the reader's obvious question ("wouldn't it still be here, only unseen?") threatens the theory, the Psychologist supplies "presentation below the threshold" on the spot.

## 3. Part by part

| Part | Mark | Why |
|---|---|---|
| P1, duration as 4th dimension | **Held** | for the job "time counts as a dimension at all" (given job). Drop it and nothing is left calling Duration a dimension. It's *built*: the instantaneous-cube point is a real, checkable piece of reasoning. |
| P2, only-perception-differs | **Held if** | held only if the added job "time has no physical asymmetry beyond how we perceive it" is granted — and that is exactly the doubtful point. Swap in a rival account of time's one-wayness (say, an irreversible physical process) and the case for *steerable* travel does not survive; so this part carries real weight, but on an untested footing. Asserted, not built. |
| P3, gravity analogy | **Loose** | swap "gravitation" for any other placeholder obstacle ("friction," "custom," "the usual order of things") and the argument reads exactly the same, because no mechanism for a time-analogue of gravity is ever named. What the swap shows is really held: the presumption that *any* fixed limit is contingent and technological. That is a different, more general claim than "gravity has a time-twin," and a much bigger one to be smuggling in unmarked. |
| P4a, the memory jump | **Idle** | removing it costs the argument nothing. It shows a mind can dwell on the past vividly, not that a body can be relocated in time. Rhetorical colour for the listeners. |
| P4b, the barometer chart | **Held**, but for a weaker job than claimed | it holds "time can be graphed along an axis" (uncontroversial) but is offered in support of "an axis along which travel can be steered." For that stronger job it is idle — you can graph a line without being able to walk back along it. |
| P5, the vanishing | **Unknown** | one unrepeated event, watched by people already split between wanting a wonder and suspecting a trick ("though it's all humbug, you know"). What would settle it: repeat it with an independent, non-human-eye record (a photographic plate, a scale under the table), and predict in advance what such a record should show. |
| P6, the threshold patch | **Fixed / catch-all with no gauge** | introduced exactly when the simpler rival (sleight of hand) is on the table, and tied to no measurement — no stated speed at which the object should become visible again, no reading that would show the patch is wrong rather than merely convenient. |

## 4. Whole-explanation checks

- **Flip.** Had the model not vanished, would P1–P4 have had to change? The text suggests not — trust in the Traveller is already a social matter ("too clever to be believed"), so a failed demonstration could just as easily be absorbed as "unfinished." That is about the audience, not the theory; kept apart on purpose.
- **Direction.** P1–P4 argue forward, from a definition of dimension to a prediction that travel is possible. P5 is read backward, from an unexplained vanishing to "hence the theory." A vanishing consistent with time-travel is equally consistent with a trick, and nothing offered here tells the two apart.
- **Answer hidden in the starting points.** P2 and P3 already contain most of the conclusion: once "the only difference is which way consciousness moves" is granted, "so movement can be redirected" follows almost from the wording of the analogy, not from anything new.
- **Pull.** P1 is modest (duration exists, call it a dimension) and easy to grant. P3 is far stronger (arbitrary technological control of that dimension). Trust earned on P1's modesty is spent on P3 without new support.
- **What the change list leaves out.** Everything here concerns consciousness or a small model moving in time; whether ordinary matter can move is not addressed until the journey itself, and the gap goes unflagged when the theory is first laid out.
- **Best rival.** The Medical Man and the Psychologist name it themselves — conjuring — and nothing here supplies a change that would tell it apart from real time travel.
- **Where parts came from.** Built: P1. Asserted: P2, P3, P6. Borrowed (an ordinary habit of plotting a quantity against time, stretched past its job): P4b.

## 5. What would tighten it most

Two changes would do the most work: (a) name an actual obstacle for time, playing the role gravitation plays for height, so P3 stops being a free-floating analogy; (b) attach a gauge to P6 — a stated reading that would show "presentation below the threshold" is being used to swallow a failure rather than describe one.

## 6. What this does not show

This does not show the argument is false, or that Wells wrote it badly — a loose argument put in a clever, half-trusted character's mouth may be exactly the effect intended, priming the reader's own doubt. That is a claim about narrative craft (the "Stories" domain), a different question from the one tested here, and I have not tested it.

## 7. One next step

Run the same tests on Chapter IV's account of the actual journey, where the theory must for the first time explain how *matter*, not just a model or a mind, moves through time (the "slipping like a vapour" / "attenuated" language) — and check whether that is a new, tested part or another asserted patch.
